notes.summary: In Fill in the Blanks you choose the word that best completes a sentence. SSC tests three things: meaning (vocabulary in context), grammar (prepositions, tense, articles) and collocation (words that naturally go together).

concepts.title: Read for clues
concepts.body:
Every blank has a clue in the sentence. Look for:
  • Contrast words — but, although, yet, despite: the blank has the opposite sense.
  • Support words — and, because, so, also: the blank continues the same sense.
  • Definitions — a phrase after a comma or dash that explains the blank.

concepts.title: Grammar first, meaning second
concepts.body: Eliminate options that do not fit grammatically (wrong part of speech, wrong tense, wrong preposition). Then choose between the remaining ones by meaning. This often leaves only one option.

concepts.title: Collocations
concepts.body: Some words simply go together in English: pay attention, make a decision, take a risk, commit a crime, heavy rain, strong tea. A synonym that 'means the same' can still be wrong if it does not collocate (do a decision is wrong).

varieties.name: Vocabulary in context
varieties.how: Find the contrast or support clue, predict a word of your own, then match it to the options.

example.q: Although he was usually talkative, at the meeting he remained ______.

varieties.name: Prepositions and grammar
varieties.how: Many verbs and adjectives take a fixed preposition. Learn the common ones: abide by, comply with, accused of, charged with, insist on, aware of.

example.q: Every citizen must abide ______ the law.

varieties.name: Collocations
varieties.how: Pick the word that native speakers naturally pair with the given noun or verb.

example.q: The doctor advised him to ______ a break from work.
steps: English says take a break, not do / make / have done a break.

tips: Predict the answer before looking at the options; it stops you from being pulled by a tempting wrong word.
If two options are synonyms of each other, often neither is correct.
Read the sentence again with your choice filled in; it must sound natural.
traps: A word with the right meaning but wrong collocation (e.g. big rain instead of heavy rain).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The new employee was not aware ______ the office rules.
questions.solution: The adjective aware takes the preposition of: aware of something.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Before buying a house, you should ______ a careful decision.
questions.solution: The natural collocation is make a decision. Do a decision or give a decision (in this sense) is not standard English.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The minister's speech was so ______ that the audience could not understand what he actually meant.
questions.solution: The audience could not understand the meaning, so the speech was unclear: ambiguous (open to more than one meaning). Lucid and concise suggest clarity; candid means frank.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The shopkeeper was charged ______ selling adulterated food.
questions.solution: The fixed phrase is charged with an offence. (Compare: accused of an offence.)

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Far from being ______ by the early failures, the young scientist became even more determined to succeed.
questions.solution: Far from being X … became more determined means she was not discouraged. The blank needs a word meaning 'discouraged': daunted. The other three are positive and break the contrast.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The police have launched an inquiry, and anyone found guilty will have to ______ the consequences.
questions.solution: The standard collocation is face the consequences. Confront with and suffer from add wrong prepositions; meet the consequences is unidiomatic.

flashcards.back: although, but, yet, despite, however, far from
